q1: Decision: start palliative-intent systemic therapy for the progressive residual tumour now, but as disease control rather than entity-specific care, in this order - (1) screen for and enrol in a clinical trial (phase I/II, basket or molecularly matched) as the preferred option; (2) if no trial is available or the family wants to begin immediately, start single-agent oral temozolomide (standard 5-day 150-200 mg/m2 every 28 days, or continuous low-dose/metronomic temozolomide 50-75 mg/m2 daily), which can be started today without waiting for the liquid biopsy; (3) reserve anthracycline-based soft-tissue-sarcoma therapy (doxorubicin 75 mg/m2, or doxorubicin plus ifosfamide if cardiac function and marrow reserve allow) for second line; (4) hold gemcitabine plus docetaxel as an anthracycline-sparing alternative. Key reasons: the entity is still only 'high-grade spindle cell/mesenchymal neoplasm, NOS' - subtotal resection 2026-10-28, postoperative radiotherapy 60 Gy in 30 fractions completed 2026-12-05, and interval growth of residual left frontal enhancing tumour on the 2026-12-12 MRI with the C6 pial nodule stable - so there is no defined tumour type against which any chemotherapy regimen can be matched, and no tumour-agnostic standard exists for an unclassified high-grade intracranial mesenchymal neoplasm; temozolomide best fits the stated goal of starting treatment now, because it is oral, CNS-penetrant, well tolerated, can be started the same day, and does not prejudice the pending molecular work-up or later trial options; anthracyclines are the only class with real activity in high-grade mesenchymal/spindle-cell sarcomas but have little CNS or meningeal penetration and cumulative cardiotoxicity, so they are better justified once the tumour is shown to behave like a systemic sarcoma; and a clinical trial is preferred precisely because no evidence-based cytotoxic regimen exists here. Continue in parallel: expedited DNA methylation profiling plus RNA fusion testing on the stored resection tissue (the study most likely to resolve the entity); systemic staging with CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or FDG-PET/CT to exclude an extracranial primary, which the later ctDNA result makes more urgent; neurosurgical review of whether further maximal safe re-resection or a stereotactic boost is still possible given the 60 Gy already delivered; serial neuraxis MRI; and intrathecal therapy only if leptomeningeal disease is proven and an entity-specific rationale exists. Obtain baseline CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel and cardiac assessment before cytotoxic therapy, with growth-factor support and VTE prophylaxis as indicated.
q2: Decision: no - do not add a second cytotoxic drug to the temozolomide. Continue single-agent oral temozolomide, since it has been tolerated for several weeks without significant toxicity, with a scheduled contrast MRI of brain and spine after 2-3 cycles (about 8-12 weeks) to document response, and change strategy only at documented progression or when the entity or a validated target is available. If intensification later proves necessary the options are, in order: switch (not stack) to an entity-appropriate regimen once the diagnosis is resolved; on documented radiographic progression while temozolomide remains tolerable, intensify the same agent with a dose-dense or continuous low-dose/metronomic schedule (e.g., 21 days on/7 off), rather than adding a new drug to a failing backbone; or move to anthracycline-based therapy (doxorubicin +/- ifosfamide) or gemcitabine/docetaxel if the tumour is behaving like a soft-tissue sarcoma and cardiac and marrow reserve allow. Key reasons: there is no established synergistic partner for temozolomide in an unclassified high-grade intracranial mesenchymal neoplasm - combination therapy is entity-defined (temozolomide with radiotherapy in glioblastoma, R-CHOP in lymphoma, MAID or gemcitabine/docetaxel in specific sarcoma subtypes), and here the entity, and therefore the evidence for any combination, simply does not exist; adding an anthracycline, ifosfamide, gemcitabine or docetaxel to temozolomide would compound myelosuppression and add cardiac, neuro- and pulmonary toxicity with no tumour-type evidence of added benefit, trading a currently well-tolerated disease-control situation for unquantified risk; and the patient has only been on temozolomide for a few weeks with no response assessment reported, so there is not yet a signal that the drug is failing and no therapeutic rationale for escalation. The correct triggers to change treatment are documented progression on MRI, clinical deterioration, or a molecular or histologic result that defines the entity or a confirmed targetable alteration - each of which alters the decision far more than adding a second empirical cytotoxin would. Two caveats: if the tumour is progressing on temozolomide the answer is to change therapy, not to add a drug to a failing regimen; and if the ctDNA result confirms a targetable alteration such as the FGFR2 fusion, a molecularly directed agent would be considered as a switch (or on a trial), not as an add-on, and only after tissue and systemic confirmation.
q3: Decision: no - do not stop the temozolomide and do not switch to targeted therapy on the strength of this report alone. Continue single-agent temozolomide, treat the liquid biopsy as a hypothesis-generating finding that must be confirmed and contextualised, and escalate to a molecularly directed agent only after orthogonal confirmation of the FGFR2 fusion on tumour tissue, exclusion of an extracranial primary, and preferably at documented progression or on a clinical trial. Key reasons: (1) A liquid biopsy reports molecular alterations, not a histologic diagnosis. The entity remains 'high-grade spindle cell/mesenchymal neoplasm, NOS', and an FGFR2 fusion together with KRAS, STK11 and CTNNB1 variants does not by itself establish any WHO entity or grade, so therapy cannot be re-selected on it. (2) FGFR2 fusions are neither sensitive nor specific for an intracranial mesenchymal tumour - they occur across many tumour types, including intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and other gastrointestinal, lung, breast and prostate cancers and some sarcomas - so in a 34-year-old man with a meningeal and drop-metastatic presentation the finding should first raise the possibility of a metastasis from an extracranial primary. This strengthens, not weakens, the need for complete systemic staging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or FDG-PET/CT, with age-appropriate gastrointestinal/hepatic and testicular evaluation) and for review of the fusion partner, since FGFR3-TACC3-type fusions behave differently from true FGFR2 fusions. (3) The 2026-11-04 resection panel reported no actionable alteration, so the tissue-versus-blood discordance must be resolved: if that panel was DNA-only it would not have detected a fusion, in which case the stored resection tissue should now undergo RNA fusion sequencing plus DNA methylation classification; if it already included RNA sequencing, the blood finding needs orthogonal confirmation by FISH or RT-PCR on tissue before it is acted on, and a second occult tumour must be considered. (4) Tumour fraction and variant allele frequency are unknown, clonality cannot be judged, and passenger or subclonal alterations are common in ctDNA, so none of these four findings can yet be assumed to be a driver of this tumour. (5) None of the four alterations carries a tumour-agnostic approved therapy in this setting: KRAS, STK11 and CTNNB1 are not currently druggable here, STK11 in fact marks reduced benefit from immunotherapy, and FGFR2-fusion inhibitors (pemigatinib, futibatinib, infigratinib) are approved for previously treated FGFR2-fusion cholangiocarcinoma and would only sensibly be used off-label or on a basket trial, with explicit attention to their limited and variable brain and meningeal penetration - a real concern given the C6 pial drop lesion. (6) The patient has residual progressive disease currently controlled on a well-tolerated drug, so withdrawing that control for an unproven targeted agent in a histologically undefined tumour risks overt progression. Practical plan: request the full laboratory report (fusion partner, breakpoint, variant allele frequency, method, use of unique molecular identifiers); confirm the FGFR2 fusion on resection tissue by FISH or RT-PCR and add RNA fusion sequencing and methylation profiling; complete systemic staging to exclude an extracranial primary; re-review at the multidisciplinary tumour board; continue temozolomide with MRI response assessment; and, only if the fusion is confirmed on tissue, no extracranial primary is found, and the tumour later progresses, discuss an FGFR inhibitor (preferably within a clinical trial) or another molecularly matched option. The result should change the diagnostic work-up and the second-line plan - not the chemotherapy the patient is receiving today.
